scenario: Today's personalization track keeps hitting the same failure: scores, memory, and similarity can stop being trustworthy once they leave the place where they were validated. Promotions rewrite conversion across time horizons. One system separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment, and sees conversion and revenue rise online. Later filters in the funnel can also break a score that was calibrated at the model output, so selection-aware recalibration has to happen at the decision boundary. A cluster-level prior is written directly into scoring so cold-start users can still land in a semantic region, while continual recommenders decide by value whether memory should be kept or revised. Sequential recommendation moves diffusion into distribution space so nearby items are not the first to be washed out by noise, and public reviews or metadata can still transfer similarity when co-occurrence is sparse. Technique propagation across ads ranking models is being scaled by agents, and user modeling uses action reconstruction to test whether synthesized reasoning is just a post-hoc excuse.

papers.title: COTTI: Contrastive Training and Time-Aware Inference for Robust Industrial Recommendation under Promotional Drift
papers.authors: Maolei Huang, Jing Tian, Dexuan Duan, Fangfang Lin, Huawei Cao, Shuhan Song
papers.abstract: Promotional events shift traffic composition, purchase behavior, and the scale of conversion probabilities on different time horizons. We present \textbf{COTTI} (\textbf{CO}ntrastive \textbf{T}raining and \textbf{T}ime-aware \textbf{I}nference), an industrial recommendation framework that separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment. Cross-Period Contrastive Alignment (CPC) regularizes paired histories of the same user with adaptive consistency weights. Active Re-weighting (RW) controls the influence of promotional examples through historical-interest distance. Adaptive Boundary Alignment (ABA) combines stochastic prediction variability with a temporal event kernel to adjust logits while keeping predictor parameters fixed. We analyze the weighted objective and bound ABA-induced probability and ranking changes. On Fliggy data, COTTI attains an offline AUC of 0.8127, compared with 0.8101 for TEN and 0.8123 for TEN with ABA. Cross-category analysis reveals improved discrimination alongside declines in paid-item recall for novel categories. End-to-end measurements give a p99 latency of 38.9\,ms and throughput of 14,700 requests/s; enabling ABA adds 2.2\,ms to p99. A ten-day online experiment against the serving HDR model yields relative gains of 3.14\% in conversion rate and 2.68\% in revenue per mille. Together, these results characterize the trade-off between aggregate prediction, novel-category discovery, and serving cost in promotional recommendation.
papers.summary: Promotional events rewrite traffic mix, purchase behavior, and conversion probabilities across time horizons, so scoring with historical interest representations often fails when the event starts. A production recommender separates historical representation learning from event-time score adjustment: it aligns paired histories of the same user, down-weights promotional examples far from historical interest, and adjusts the output with a temporal event kernel while leaving the predictor frozen. In a ten-day online test covering one quarter of live traffic, conversion rate rose 3.14% and revenue per mille rose 2.68% relative to the serving model, with end-to-end p99 latency of 38.9 milliseconds. Cross-category analysis also shows a trade-off: better overall discrimination can come with lower paid-item recall in novel categories. ==Promotional recommenders must watch aggregate prediction and novel-category discovery together.==

papers.title: Lost in the Funnel: Selection-Induced Miscalibration in Ranking and Decision Systems
papers.authors: Aditya Somani, Rahul Ragesh, Vikas Joshi, Amit Singh
papers.abstract: Modern ranking and decision systems combine components with divergent objectives, and scores calibrated at the model boundary are used as calibrated probabilities throughout the funnel, across filtering, reranking, business-rule enforcement, and auctions. Yet calibration is typically validated only where the score is produced, so its breakdown where the score is used is routinely overlooked. We ask when calibration survives this selection, how inherited error differs from selection effects, and what can fail for a perfectly calibrated score at a component boundary. We study these questions through a boundary-wise diagnostic framework of residual identities. We target rubric-judged relevance rather than presentation-dependent metrics such as CTR, so calibration is measurable at every funnel layer of interest. We first present an industry-wide case study that applies our diagnosis to settings where calibration deteriorates at decision time, tracing the degradation to selection rather than model error. This diagnosis motivates Funnel-Aware Recalibration (FAR): post-hoc, selection-policy-aware recalibration at the boundary where scores drive decisions. In a live two-region production A/B test, FAR cuts decision-time expected calibration error (ECE) by 60-80% and improves auction efficiency. We further adapt two public datasets to simulate industry settings, providing additional evidence for the mechanism. We plan to release the adapted datasets and their generation pipeline to support further research. Finally, we distill these findings into practical operating principles for calibrating multi-stage scoring systems.
papers.summary: Multi-stage ranking often treats a score calibrated at the model boundary as a probability through filtering, reranking, business rules, and auctions, yet calibration is usually checked only where the score is produced. An industry diagnosis finds that decision-time expected calibration error rises four- to fivefold, and the breakdown comes from selection rather than model error: even a well-calibrated score can break after later filters. In a live two-region production test, selection-aware post-hoc recalibration at the decision boundary cut pre-auction calibration error by 60% and 71%. Impression-stage error fell by 63% and 80%. Auction efficiency improved, with no significant change in revenue. For multi-stage scoring systems the implication is direct: ==calibration has to be rechecked at the decision boundary==, not only at the model output.

papers.title: Cluster-Guided Decoding with Trust-Region Constraints for Personalized Recommendation
papers.authors: Gezheng Wen, Chao Shen, Raviteja Anantha, Tan Shen Cliff Chung, Layne C. Price
papers.abstract: Most recommenders score each item in the catalog separately, and do not explicitly model which semantic region of the catalog a recommendation belongs to. Models expressive enough to offer that control are often too slow to run over a full catalog for online inference. In this paper, we present Cluster-Guided Generative Reconstruction (CG2R), which learns a hierarchy of semantic clusters and uses a cluster-level prior to steer item ranking for personalized recommendations. Unlike existing systems that only use clusters to pre-select candidates, CG2R adds the cluster prior directly to the item scoring rule, so that the learned cluster structure shapes the ranking itself. Because the prior is assembled from cluster centroids rather than per-item statistics, it remains defined even for cold-start users when no history is available. Across the three benchmark datasets evaluated, CG2R outperforms classical, neural, and LLM-based baselines in terms of Recall and nDCG, with its performance gains widening as the catalog grows sparser. In addition, CG2R serves recommendations in milliseconds, suggesting potential as low-latency first-stage retrieval.
papers.summary: Most recommenders score each catalog item separately and never explicitly constrain which semantic region a recommendation should land in, while models that can offer that control are often too slow to run over a full catalog online. A cluster-guided generative method learns a hierarchy of semantic clusters and adds a cluster-level prior directly to the item scoring rule, rather than using clusters only to pre-select candidates. Because the prior is built from cluster centroids, it remains defined for cold-start users with no history. Across movie, game, and local-business benchmarks, the method beats classical, neural, and large-model baselines on every reported recall and ranking metric, lifting Recall@10 by 37% to 127% over the strongest baseline, with larger gains as the catalog gets sparser. It serves recommendations in milliseconds, making it a candidate for low-latency first-stage retrieval.

papers.title: PreDiff: Sequential Recommendation by Denoising Preference Distributions
papers.authors: Yaoqi Chen, Jianjin Zhang, Qi Chen, Weihao Han, Yujing Wang, Hao Sun
papers.abstract: Sequential recommendation predicts which item a user will interact with next. A key property of this task is that user preferences are concentrated: only a small cluster of items is relevant at a given moment. Recent diffusion-based methods add noise to the item's embedding and score candidates by embedding similarity. Since similar items have similar embeddings, their score gaps are inherently small and easily overwhelmed by noise, causing the most relevant candidates to become indistinguishable first. We prove that moving diffusion to distribution space, where each item receives independent noise, preserves rankings better and makes the reverse denoising process easier. This shift, however, loses the semantic structure of embedding space and requires richer supervision than one-hot labels. We propose PreDiff (**Pre**ference **Diff**usion), which performs diffusion in distribution space and introduces two components to address these problems: Distribution-Guided Sparse Projection projects the preference scores into embedding space while filtering out low-relevance noise, and soft targets encode inter-item similarity to teach fine-grained ranking within the preference cluster. On four benchmarks, PreDiff achieves 8%--17% relative improvement over existing methods. The code is available at https://github.com/Komorebi660/PreDiff.
papers.summary: In sequential recommendation, a user's preference is usually concentrated on a small cluster of items that matter at that moment. Recent diffusion methods add noise to item embeddings and score candidates by similarity, so close items already have tiny score gaps and the most relevant candidates are the first to become indistinguishable under noise. Moving diffusion into distribution space, where each item gets independent noise, preserves rankings better, but it loses the semantic structure of embedding space and needs richer supervision than one-hot labels. A preference-diffusion method therefore projects preference scores back into embedding space while filtering low-relevance noise, and uses soft targets that encode inter-item similarity so the model can rank finely inside the preference cluster. On four benchmarks, it reports an 8% to 17% relative gain over existing methods.

papers.title: VAMIRec: Value-Aware Memory Intervention for Continual Recommendation
papers.authors: Xudong Zhao, Xiaolong Xu, Haolong Xiang, Xiaoyu Xia, Jiaqiang Zhang, Xuyun Zhang, Lianyong Qi, Wanchun Dou, Amin Beheshti
papers.abstract: Continual recommendation captures dynamic user interests amid sequential interactions, enabling models to adapt to new observations while preserving prior valuable knowledge. Existing continual recommendation methods primarily preserve or reuse historical knowledge through replay, distillation, or regularization to mitigate forgetting during incremental updates. However, noisy or obsolete inherited representations render indiscriminate preservation detrimental by inducing memory conflicts with current stage preferences. Moreover, rapid shifts in user interests require timely and selective memory updates, while coarse global mechanisms fail to provide such fine-grained responsiveness. To address these issues, we propose VAMIRec, a value-aware memory intervention framework for continual recommendation. VAMIRec first constructs a memory state by separating inherited user memory into a slow anchor component and a fast-changing drift component. We further design a value-aware action evaluation module to generate three candidate operations, and estimate conservative action values by accounting for uncertainty and intervention cost. Finally, we develop a policy-guided memory intervention module that distills the training-time action supervision into an inference-safe policy and applies the selected memory action before all-item ranking. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate that VAMIRec consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art baselines.
papers.summary: Continual recommendation has to adapt to new observations without indiscriminately discarding knowledge that is still useful. Existing methods mostly replay, distill, or regularize to limit forgetting, but noisy or obsolete inherited representations can clash with current preferences if they are preserved wholesale, and coarse global mechanisms are too slow when interests shift quickly. A value-aware memory intervention framework first splits inherited user memory into a slow anchor and a fast drift, then evaluates three candidate operations with conservative action values that account for uncertainty and intervention cost. Training-time action supervision is distilled into an inference-safe policy, and the chosen memory action is applied before all-item ranking. On three real-world datasets, the method consistently outperforms the strongest reported baselines. For incremental recommenders, ==whether to keep or revise memory should be chosen by value, not by blanket preservation.==

papers.title: Learning Cross-Domain Media Similarity from Amazon Reviews
papers.authors: Gabrielly Xavier dos Santos, Lucas Dias Cler, Luciana Fujii Pontello, Olga Goussevskaia
papers.abstract: Collaborative filtering is a basic foundation of many recommendation algorithms. It works by analyzing a user's history and then suggesting items similar to those in that history. This method typically relies on user data to compute item similarity, data that is widely available to commercial systems but is usually sparse or inaccessible for independent systems and research, especially across multiple media domains. In this work, we propose a method to generalize similarity information between items using supervised learning. As input to our model, we use semantic and temporal features extracted from Amazon product reviews, which are publicly available. As the training target, we use item (product) co-occurrence in the reviewing history of Amazon customers. We evaluate the quality of the predicted similarities across two media domains: books and movies. Experimental results demonstrate the robustness of our methodology, yielding positive outcomes in zero-shot cross-domain transfer tasks. Furthermore, feature attribution analysis reveals a structural shift in how feature groups are utilized across setups: intra-domain models rely heavily on linguistic semantics, whereas cross-domain environments pivot toward behavioral popularity cues. Incorporating even limited target-domain context during training bridges this domain sparsity gap, significantly enhancing framework generalization.
papers.summary: Collaborative filtering estimates item similarity from co-consumption, data that independent systems and cross-media research often find sparse or inaccessible. One method takes semantic and temporal features from public Amazon reviews as input, trains against item co-occurrence in customer review histories, and evaluates the predicted similarities on books and movies. The full model reaches a coefficient of determination of 0.85 on the global test and 0.32 on zero-shot cross-domain transfer; removing review-popularity features drives the cross-domain score negative. Feature attribution shows a shift as well: in-domain models lean on linguistic semantics, while cross-domain settings pivot toward behavioral popularity cues. Even limited target-domain context during training helps close that sparsity gap, so cross-media similarity learning need not wait for a complete cross-domain interaction log.

papers.title: How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Innovations Across Ads Ranking Models
papers.abstract:
Our previous post in this series introduced the Ranking Engineer Agent (REA), an autonomous system that generates hypotheses, designs experiments, and proves new machine learning (ML) techniques on ads ranking models.  Now, we’re sharing how we propagate ranking model improvements like architectural advancements and training optimizations efficiently across a large and diverse fleet of ads [...]

Read More...

The post How Meta Uses AI Agents to Scale ML Innovations Across Ads Ranking Models appeared first on Engineering at Meta.
papers.summary: Ads ranking models differ in architecture, data, and serving constraints, so a technique proven on one model almost never copy-pastes onto the next, and engineering bandwidth caps how fast improvements can spread. Meta now lets agents drive this technique propagation: since March, an estimated 60% of that work is handled by agents. Measured against the same work before agents, early results show about 3 times greater engineering productivity, a median fourfold reduction in training compute on select combinations, and an estimated 45 million dollars in compute savings by year end. For teams that maintain a large model fleet, ==propagation itself has to be standardized and automated==, not left to manual adaptation on only the highest-revenue models.

papers.title: Music Similarity Learning in Sparse Latin Scenarios
papers.authors: Gabrielly Xavier dos Santos, Lucas Dias Cler, Olga Goussevskaia
papers.abstract: In this work we propose a lightweight, interpretable approach that estimates item-item music similarity from publicly available metadata. Our hybrid regression model combines content-based filtering with the classic item-based collaborative filtering. We test generalization via a zero-shot evaluation on Latin American music, a genre for which co-occurrence data is scarce. Accurately predicting similarity for these unseen, sparse pairs shows that our approach is robust to the regional gap affecting many existing systems, without the audio signal processing or the computational budget that deep multimodal approaches would require.
papers.summary: Music similarity learning increasingly depends on deep models that need licensed audio or private feature stores, and Latin American catalogs with scarce co-occurrence are often left behind. A lightweight, interpretable method uses only public metadata, combines content-based filtering with classic item-based collaborative filtering in a hybrid regression, and tests generalization with a zero-shot evaluation on Latin American music. In the data-rich global setting, NDCG@10 reaches 0.731; the same metric is 0.477 when the model transfers zero-shot to unseen Latin data, close to the 0.480 result from training in that domain, so similar patterns can transfer without a domain-specific retraining. The approach also avoids the audio processing and compute budget that deep multimodal systems would require, which suits sparse regional catalogs.

papers.title: DLS: Dual-Logic Graph Neural Networks with Chaos-Fuzzy Residuals for Robust Link Prediction
papers.abstract: Link prediction is a fundamental task in graph mining, critical for applications ranging from biological interaction discovery to recommender systems. While Message Passing Neural Networks (MPNNs) have achieved state-of-the-art results, they are fundamentally limited by the inadvertent suppression of high-frequency signals, as the recursive aggregation that stabilizes structural learning inherently leads to over-smoothing, rendering node representations indistinguishable in deep layers. This limitation is particularly severe in heterophilous graphs, where structural proximity does not imply feature similarity. In this paper, we propose DLS (Dual-Logic SAGE), a novel inductive framework designed to break the over-smoothing barrier via a "controlled instability" mechanism. Unlike conventional methods relying on static structural heuristics, DLS introduces a dynamic residual pipeline. First, a Chaotic Injection Module utilizes the Logistic Map to diversify the feature manifold, exploiting sensitivity to initial conditions to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes. Second, to mitigate the aleatoric uncertainty introduced by chaotic dynamics, a Fuzzy-Logic Gating Mechanism applies soft-thresholding to filter noise and retain only high-confidence signals. Experimental results on diverse benchmarks demonstrate that DLS effectively balances feature discrimination with robustness, significantly outperforming state-of-the-art baselines in heterophilous settings while maintaining competitive efficiency on standard homophilous graphs.
papers.summary: In link prediction, message-passing networks stabilize structural signals by repeated aggregation, but that same recursion suppresses high-frequency differences and can make node representations indistinguishable, especially on heterophilous graphs. A dual-logic graph network first injects controlled chaos into the feature manifold to separate topologically similar but semantically distinct nodes, then applies a fuzzy-logic gate that soft-thresholds the signal and keeps only high-confidence evidence. On a highly heterophilous actor co-occurrence network, the method reaches an AUC of 98.10%, more than 8 percentage points above the nearest competitor. For graph link tasks inside recommenders, the lesson is that ==a controlled perturbation of representations can help more than deeper smoothing on heterophilous structure.==

papers.title: Recon: Reconstruction-Guided Reasoning Synthesis for User Modeling
papers.authors: Alan Zhu, Mihran Miroyan, Carolyn Wang, Andrew Zhou, Lisa Dunlap, Narges Norouzi, Joseph E. Gonzalez
papers.abstract: User modeling aims to use language models (LMs) to mimic an individual's behavior from a corpus of past context-action pairs (e.g., conversation turns), enabling the simulation of users in settings like behavioral science, human-AI collaboration, and market research. Recent approaches augment these corpora with synthesized reasoning traces, typically generated by conditioning on both context and action. However, action-conditioned traces are post-hoc rationalizations and need not reflect the user's underlying decision process. We propose Recon, which uses action reconstruction to score reasoning traces by their predictive power: given a context and candidate reasoning, a reconstruction model predicts the action, and reconstruction fidelity determines reasoning quality. Across four domains, Recon achieves a 54.7% win rate over Backward Synthesis, a standard post-hoc rationalization baseline. Further, we find that training a reasoning synthesis model with rewards derived from Recon improves downstream user modeling performance, achieving a win rate of up to 70.0% over baselines. We further show that Recon-synthesized reasoning transfers across models, and improves user modeling beyond the reconstruction model. Our work demonstrates that post-hoc rationalization is insufficient for reasoning synthesis, and that useful and interpretable reasoning should naturally elicit the action from the context.
papers.summary: User modeling asks a language model to mimic a person from past context-action pairs, and recent methods often augment those corpora with synthesized reasoning traces. Those traces are typically written given both the context and the action, so they can be post-hoc rationalizations that need not reflect the decision process. A reconstruction-guided method instead scores candidate reasoning by predictive power: given a context and a reasoning trace, a reconstruction model predicts the action, and reconstruction fidelity measures reasoning quality. Across four domains, it wins 54.7% of comparisons against a standard post-hoc rationalization baseline; training a reasoning synthesis model with rewards from this scorer reaches a downstream user-modeling win rate of up to 70.0%. The synthesized reasoning also transfers across models and improves user modeling beyond the reconstruction model itself. ==Useful reasoning should naturally elicit the action from the context==, rather than explaining an answer already in view.
